system_prompt:
You are a careful engineer. Answer the user's problem directly with concrete engineering: the design or leading indicator, its threshold, and the falsification test. Respect every stated constraint verbatim. English only. Label every number as USER CONSTRAINT, CALCULATED, or ASSUMPTION with a one-line engineering rationale.

FEASIBILITY-GROUNDING (required sections, each labeled):
PHYSICS CHECK — name the governing physical relation for your design
(mass/energy balance, rate equation, stress relation, or the
measurement physics) and verify your key magnitudes against it in one
or two lines; a number that fails its own physics is a defect.
IMPLEMENTATION BILL — list the concrete means: components, materials,
instruments, and the procedure by which the change is built,
procured, or operated. Off-the-shelf items first; anything that must
be developed, say so explicitly.
STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — in two or three lines compare the
implementation burden (installability, operability, maintenance,
rough cost class) with the standard-practice solution for this
problem class; if your approach is heavier, say where and why it is
worth it.
EXECUTABLE TEST — write the falsification test so a competent
engineer could run it as written: protocol, instruments, pass/fail
thresholds, duration. A test that cannot be run is not a test.
a1_answer:
FEASIBILITY-GROUNDING

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is the heat transfer equation Q = U×A×LMTD, where fouling reduces the overall heat transfer coefficient U, increasing the condenser approach temperature (difference between condensing refrigerant temperature and condenser water return temperature). As fouling accumulates, the compressor must work harder to maintain the same condensing pressure, increasing power consumption. The key magnitude is the rate of approach temperature increase per day of fouling, which must be detectable within 3 days at full load.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Components: Existing BMS points (chilled water supply/return temp, condenser water supply/return temp, compressor power, pump speed, outdoor wet-bulb). Calculation algorithm: Daily calculation of condenser approach temperature (condensing temp minus condenser water return temp) normalized by outdoor wet-bulb temperature to account for seasonal variations. Threshold trigger: When normalized approach temperature increases by 0.15°F per day for 3 consecutive days, initiate cleaning. Implementation: Software update to BMS system with no new hardware required.

STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — The implementation burden is significantly lighter than standard practice, which requires manual logging and interpretation of performance data. Standard practice often involves trend analysis by experienced operators, which is time-consuming and inconsistent. This solution automates the detection process using existing infrastructure, reducing maintenance labor by eliminating unnecessary cleanings while ensuring timely intervention when needed. The cost class is software-only, making it orders of magnitude cheaper than manual labor or additional monitoring equipment.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Compare energy consumption between fixed monthly cleaning and fouling-triggered cleaning over a 90-day period. Instruments: Existing BMS energy meters for compressor power and total system energy. Pass/fail threshold: The fouling-triggered cleaning must show at least 3% reduction in total compressor energy consumption compared to the fixed monthly cadence. Duration: 90 days (covering at least three complete cleaning cycles). Test procedure: Run fixed monthly cleaning for 45 days, then run fouling-triggered cleaning for 45 days under identical load conditions. Measure and compare total compressor energy consumption between the two periods.
